title: Helical stability of double-stranded semiflexible chains with interstrand interactions
authors: Farisan Dary, Donn Liew, Haiyi Liang, Ee Hou Yong
abstract: The mechanical and structural properties of dsDNA have been successfully described by models with varying levels of complexity and coarse-graining schemes. Prior work has characterized local stacking/twist effects and force-torque phase diagrams under external constraints. However, the role of base-pairing and torsional elasticity in global morphological transitions remain poorly characterized in the absence of external constraints. Here we investigate the delicate balance required for the strength of base-pairing interactions and the twisting energy to preserve the double-helix structure in a model made up of two semiflexible chains. We found that the model exhibits several distinct morphological phases: flat, random coil, double-helix, and the unwound double-helix. We calculate the Gauss linking number to characterize transitions between these phases.
summary: This work models double-stranded semiflexible chains to understand how base-pairing and twisting energies dictate the overall helical structure. Using Monte Carlo simulations, the authors map out distinct morphological phases—including unwinding transitions—by tracking topological invariants like the Gauss linking number. The findings elucidate a delicate energetic balance governing structural stability in biopolymer systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the global morphological transitions of double-stranded semiflexible chains, specifically determining the balance required between base-pairing interactions and twisting energy to maintain the double-helix structure without external constraints.
main_result: The model exhibits distinct phases (flat, random coil, double-helix, unwound) whose transitions are characterized by first-order changes in linking number. The system's stability is governed by minimizing total energy across these competing structural states.
method: Monte Carlo simulations using the Metropolis algorithm were employed to sample configurations based on a Hamiltonian incorporating bending, pairing, and twisting energies.
model_or_system: The physical system is modeled as two semiflexible chains interacting via base-pairing ($E_{	ext{pair}}$) and diagonal interactions ($E_{	ext{diag}}$), with handedness regulated by $E_{	ext{twist}}$. The total energy includes bending terms derived from the Kratky-Porod potential.
key_observables: Gauss linking number ($	ext{Lk}$), Order Parameter ($	ext{Nu/N}$), correlation functions ($\langle t_n \cdot t_0 angle$, $\langle c_n \cdot c_0 angle$), and average energy per segment ($\epsilon$).
important_parameters: Interaction strengths ($D$ for base-stacking, $P$ for twist symmetry breaking) and the dimensionless temperature parameter ($\Lambda = T/T_0$).
main_assumptions: Bending flexibility is assumed to follow the Kratky-Porod potential. The analysis relies on fitting correlation functions to damped oscillatory forms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate distinct morphologies based on varying interaction parameters ($P$ and $D$), plot the linking number ($	ext{Lk}(n)$) across different phases, and show temperature dependence of persistence lengths.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the model Hamiltonian, uses Monte Carlo simulations to map out phase diagrams based on coupling constants ($D, P$), analyzes topological invariants like the linking number to pinpoint transitions, and finally examines thermal effects via correlation functions.
why_interesting: While focused on biophysics (DNA), the methodology—using statistical mechanics tools like phase transition analysis, energy minimization across competing structural states, and topological diagnostics ($	ext{Lk}$)—is highly relevant for understanding complex many-body systems in AMO physics or quantum materials where local interactions drive global order.

The vertices {ri} are connected by tangent vector, i.e., ri+1 = ri + ∆· ti. The parameters r0 diag r0 pair are the equilibrium distance of pairs that are direct opposite and di- agonal opposite of each other, respectively. (b) A schematic diagram showing the counterclockwise rotation of successive corresponding vectors {ci} and the triangular planes whose normals are used to regulate the twist.

FIG. 2. A schematic diagram of a chain generating algorithm. The subsequent tangent vector ti+1 is determined as the pro- jection of the resultant vector of preceding tangent vector ti and displacement vector tan θ ˆd onto the surface of a unit sphere.

FIG. 3. Morphologically distinct configurations obtained from different values of P and D. The flat configuration corre- sponds to P = D = 0, while the random coil configuration corresponds to P = 0 and nonzero D. When both parame- ters are nonzero, the configuration adopts three different mor- phologies depending on the magnitude of P and D.

FIG. 4. The cumulative link function Lk(n) of configurations in different morphological phases. The link in double-helix phase (red) and during the transition (green) from flat to double-helix is linearly increasing along the configuration. In unwound double-helix phase, the nonlinear trends in Lk(n) corresponds to a ladder-like configuration. The link is rela- tively small in the flat phase (lavender) since the configura- tion rarely bends and twists. In the random coil phase (blue), Lk(n) fluctuates between positive and negative link since the configuration is allowed to twist freely in any direction since the handedness-symmetry is unbroken.

FIG. 5. Morphological phases of the model with different values of P and D: (a) When D = 10 is fixed, the configuration becomes right-handed spontaneously when P is no longer zero. The configuration is a partially unwound double-helix (yellow →), which eventually becomes full double-helix (red →) as P increases further. (b) When P = 1 fixed, the configuration with D = 0 has nonzero linking number (green →), which steadily (signified by the gradual rise in the Gauss link) becomes a double-helix as as D increases.
